Radial sources and quadratic logarithms

Reconstructed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

The equation away from a singular point does not determine the source at that point. We calculate that source by integrating over a small surrounding sphere. This produces complex quadratic logarithms, inverses of the squared Laplacian, entire families of radial exponentials, and the point term in their second derivatives.

Throughout, , distributions act complex-linearly on , and integration uses ordinary Lebesgue density. Set and . The earlier programme proofs used below, including the foundations of integration and matrix algebra, are identified at the end. Every additional identity needed here is proved below.

The complete integral Taylor proof supplies the finite-order remainders used here, including signed increments, complex-valued functions, directional derivatives and uniform bounds for all required derivatives on compact neighborhoods.

The convergent exponential series, differentiated with respect to the scalar , proves and near zero. Away from zero its Hessian is which is locally integrable. Integration by parts outside a small ball proves that these are the full weak derivatives. For the first derivative the error is bounded by the area times bounded and the test; for the second it is bounded by the same area times the bounded gradient and test. Both errors tend to zero. Thus this remainder contributes no point term.

We now prove the Newton Hessian explicitly. The weak first derivative, already established in U020, Theorem 1.1, is , a locally integrable function. Its classical -derivative away from zero is . Sphere symmetries give : reflection reverses an off-diagonal integrand, permutation makes the three diagonal integrals equal, and their sum is . Programme proof locations and freely accessible sources

The following are exact earlier programme proofs used in this lesson. The supplied foundation files retain their own license notices.

  • Boundary flux and weak identities, Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2: surface measure, divergence and Green identities on the punctured regions used here.
  • Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 3.1: full Newton sources and first weak gradients, real symmetric diagonalization, the matrix determinant branch and its semidefinite extension, and the complex Gaussian mass.
  • Homogeneous extensions and angular moments, Lemma 1.1: the Euler characterization of homogeneity. The rotation-to-constant argument needed here is proved in Solution 4 above.
  • Convolution as addition of supports, Theorem 1.1, Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 5.2: compact-support convolution, differentiation, local smoothing and convergence.
  • Gluing holomorphic sides, Lemma 3.2: the scalar identity principle for the optional continuation check after (3.5).
  • Causal integration of complex order, scalar logarithm construction immediately before Theorem 4.1: local logarithmic series and slit-plane branch. The branch change used here is specified before Theorem 1.1.
  • Scalar and metric foundations, §§12–13: compactness, calculus, exponential and trigonometric series, and smooth cutoffs.
  • Finite-dimensional foundations, §10: matrix inverses, adjugates, determinants and Gram surface density.
  • Integration foundations, §§15.1–15.4: convergence, Fubini, linear substitutions, approximation and mollification.
  • Angular foundations, A4–A5: polar integration and sphere areas, including .
